newsitem.title: GERMANY: Vietnam veteran tipped to head U.S. Zaire mission.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam veteran tipped to head U.S. Zaire mission.

text.p: A Vietnam war paratrooper is likely to be named as head of the American contingent of forces expected to join a proposed international mission to Zaire, a U.S. military official said on Friday.

The official at the U.S. European Command in Stuttgart, who asked not to be identified, named Major General Ed Smith, currently in charge of the U.S. army's Southern European Task Force in Italy, as likely to lead the troops.
Smith was in Central Africa on Friday leading a vanguard of some 40 American soldiers who are laying the groundwork for the U.S. forces.
"It seems very reasonable that if General Smith is now in the region and commands the Southern task force, that he will also be named to command the U.S. forces," the official said.

Soldiers from the unit commanded by Smith, a 51-year-old who earned the Purple Heart medal for injuries suffered in Vietnam, have been tapped to provide initial security for the deployment of up to 4,000 U.S. troops as part of the Canadian-led mission.
About 1,000 U.S. ground troops -- including about 600 paratroopers from Italy -- are expected to be sent to Zaire within days to help around 1.5 million refugees.
The refugees are mainly ethnic Hutus who fled Rwanda in 1994 amid fears of reprisals after the massacre of up to a million Tutsis and Hutu moderates.
A further 2,000 to 3,000 American troops are expected to go to nearby countries to help with support activities.

Smith's paratroopers were also among the first U.S. troops sent to Bosnia before the main deployment of some 15,000 American forces as part of an international peacekeeping effort to enforce the Dayton peace accord.
President Bill Clinton has said the U.S. commander named for the mission will be in charge of all American troops but will report to the mulitnational force leader.
Pentagon officials have said the mission will probably last for around four months and the troops will have "very robust rules of engagement" to protect themselves.

Military planners at the European Command in Stuttgart, which controls all U.S. military operations in Europe, most of the Middle East and Africa, were drawing up plans for forces to leave within hours of Clinton giving final approval.

U.S. troops are expected to provide security at the Goma airport in Zaire and along a three-mile corridor from the airport into the Rwandan city of Kigali and also provide support to humanitarian rescue efforts, the officials said.
The Zaire mission comes at a busy time for the European Command, which currently has nearly 20 percent of its force in peacekeeping missions in Bosnia, Macedonia and Turkey.
"We are very busy but we are not over-extended," one military official said, while acknowledging that forces controlled by the command have been severely cut since the end of the Cold War.
